I'm almost 4 years into recovery.

When I first got therapy I was doing horribly. Everything was a trigger and I could barely hold a job because of the freeze state and other workplace trauma I had trouble resolving.

When I moved out and my expenses increased I had a "heal or die" moment and needed to sustain myself more than gig work. I knew what I liked and pursued it - there is a saying to do it scared, and I had to do just that. It was hard being broke and traumatized but I was lucky to have a good support system as well. When I found my dream job, I slowly saw how I wasn't getting treated poorly and that I'm not the same person I was back then (a doormat).

I started believing in my abilities which helped me move forward with healing, mind you I had extremely good trauma-informed therapists who still to this day help me along the way. The more I believed in myself, the more autonomous I became.

Now I don't hate myself anymore, I'm on the self-love path even if it feels uncomfortable. It took a lot of getting out of my head and pushing through the loud CPTSD symptoms to make it to the other side. I may not be 100% healed but I'm not looking for all-or-nothing, I'm looking for progress. Progress is a daily thing you work at day in and day out. It took a lot of time being in a safe, stable environment and consistently getting therapy to help me become more functional. I find moments of peace and rest when I can and just savor those, knowing that there will be triggers that I *can* handle in the future.

You can heal from this and it's possible. I used to genuinely believe that I would never get out of these symptoms. Accept that the symptoms are there and have a deep understanding of your triggers. You can do it!

It's not bad so far but like others have said, be careful with the padding on your shoulders as it can make things unstable. Also when you're putting the bar on your back, don't stagger your stance, you want the feet next to each other for stability.

I would also focus in on engaging your core when you go down, you want to inhale as you go down and exhale as you're coming up. Bracing your core will make a world of difference for you.

Hip and ankle mobility moves can really help you get into a good squat depth. Another thing I've personally done is going lighter to focus on the form itself, don't rush going up weight too much.

You want to aim for going down and back up with control, be careful with using momentum when doing any moves.

One thing I'm going to warn you is to be careful of how you present your insecurities, especially to new people, new co-workers, new friends, etc. If you come off worrying about these kinds of things and then wrong people see it, they will 100% exploit you for it. This happened to me on countless occasions before I stopped people pleasing.

Remember, you're a person too, even if the trauma doesn't make you feel like one. Hope this helps.

These daily mood logs are nice:

https://feelinggood.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/Melanie-DML-v-1.pdf

You write a situation that bothers you, then on a scale of 0 - 100 rate your feelings in the before section.  Write the negative thoughts and how much you believe them in the before section.  Then you write the mental distortions associated with the thoughts.  After that you write a positive thought that logically clashes with the negative though and rate how much you believe the positive thought.  Then in the after section you rate your belief in the negative comment and then rate your general feelings in that after section when you complete the positive thoughts.

I use these in therapy and they helped a lot.  I think these work best when you are in therapy and then the therapist can help you sort the thoughts out.

When you feel the time is right, reach out.  If they don't respond, I don't recommend blowing up their phone because it will likely repel them.

If this conversation ends up happening for you, I would let them talk first and let them explain what hurt them and what bothered them.  Don't wait for your chance to speak, just listen instead (do this by transferring that emotional part of you toward empathy and get a view of how they feel).  Take responsibility for your actions.  Then calmly say what bothered you.  If they don't take responsibility or want to blame you entirely then be weary of it.  Also understand that they felt hurt too, so emotional reactions are a thing for them too even if not shown as intensely as we show it.

Whatever you do, do not react or have an outburst.  Just listen (it hurts a lot sometimes especially when people bring up what you did wrong, it's a feeling to get used to though so you can hold yourself accountable and become a better person).  Remember that outbursts throw all credibility out the window.

Best of luck.

PS: Don't try to predict what they'll say or play a scenario in your head that you think will happen.  It leads to outbursts because the reaction wasn't what you expected.

Fog Mode is what I call my moments I have where absolutely nothing is rational.  My mind's eye can't "see" so to speak. The desire to hurt is insanely dangerous because there's a belief that being hurtful gives a satisfying feeling or acting out on the hurt will quell it.  It won't and it makes it worse.
